core.text: To tell what *was happening* or *used to happen*, Latin slips *-ba-* between the stem and the person endings: **the imperfect (the 'was doing' tense)**. *amā-ba-t* — he was loving, he loved (over a stretch of time); *habitā-ba-nt* — they were living. The endings are *-bam, -bās, -bat, -bāmus, -bātis, -bant*; the first person uses *-m*, not *-ō*. The 1st and 2nd conjugations add *-ba-* straight to the stem vowel (*amābat, vidēbat*); the 3rd and 4th put an *-ē-* first (*scrībēbat, dormiēbat*). Latin name: imperfectum indicātīvī āctīvī.
The English past has several shapes: *I walked* (one event), *I was walking* (in progress), *I used to walk* (habit). The imperfect covers the last two.
Stem (+ ē for the 3rd and 4th) + ba + -m, -s, -t, -mus, -tis, -nt.

invented.en: The boys were playing in the garden.

core.text: Both are past. The imperfect *amābat* paints a state or habit — he loved her, was loving her; the perfect (the 'did / has done' tense) *amāvit* reports a finished event — he fell in love. Setting is imperfect; what happened next is perfect. Look for *-ba-* against a perfect stem (*-v-, -s-, -u-*).

more.text: *-bā-* is long before *-s, -mus, -tis* (*amābās, amābāmus*) and short before *-m, -t, -nt*. It is the tense of background, habit and the setting of a story. Besides *was doing*, it can mean *began to* or *tried to* (*clāmābat* — began to shout) and is the tense of description in a narrative. The imperfect of *esse* is *eram*: see the irregular imperfect.

The learner's notes (week 19): Latin shows tense with an intermediate ending between the stem and the person ending; the imperfect is one of three past tenses, for ongoing or repeated action and for setting the scene for the main events (*I was walking down the street, when…*; *I used to walk…*); the marker *(e)ba* loses its *e* after *a-* and *e-*stems and keeps it after *(i)-* and *i-*stems (*pōnēbam, pulsābam, vidēbam, fugiēbam, veniēbam*); the person endings lose their variable vowels after the *a*, and the first person always uses *-m*.

Ørberg (chapter XIX): tempus praeteritum, 3rd person *-bat / -bant*, *-ēbat / -ēbant*; *computābat, pārēbat, scrībēbat, dormiēbat*; *ante vīgintī annōs Iūlius in lūdō dormiēbat, male computābat, foedē scrībēbat*. A&G §470–471 list the uses: continued action, repeated action, description, and the 'was beginning to' sense.
